titre.sous: simple past, past continuous, past perfect

ex1.kicker: Two actions at the same moment

aparte.texte: had + past participle = earlier in the past

q.lu: By the time Mr. Ito arrived, the train ------- .

options.raison: Linked to now, not to the past

etapes.texte: __by the time, before, already__ + past: past perfect

phrases.texte: English has three main past tenses. The simple past is for a finished action: she signed the contract.
The past continuous is for an action in progress: she was reading the contract.
The past perfect is for an action before another past action: she had read it before.
Look at two actions at the same moment. I was working when the power went out.
The long action is in the past continuous. The short action that interrupts is in the simple past.
Now, one action before another. When I arrived, the meeting had already started.
The meeting started first. So we use had, plus the past participle.
Now, a TOEIC question. By the time Mr. Ito arrived, the train, blank.
phrases.dit: Now, a TOEIC question. By the time Mister Ito arrived, the train, blank.

phrases.texte: A: leaves. B: has left. C: had left. D: was leaving.
phrases.dit: Answer A. leaves. Answer B. has left. Answer C. had left. Answer D. was leaving.

phrases.texte: By the time, with a verb in the past, tells you one action happened before another.
phrases.dit: By the time, with a verb in the past, tells you one action happened before another.

phrases.texte: A is present. B links to now, not to the past. D is an action in progress.
phrases.dit: A is present. B links to now, not to the past. D is an action in progress.

phrases.texte: C is correct: by the time Mr. Ito arrived, the train had left.
phrases.dit: C is correct: by the time Mister Ito arrived, the train had left.

phrases.texte: Three steps. One: yesterday, last week and ago go with the simple past.
Two: while, or when with an interruption, goes with the past continuous.
Three: by the time, before and already, with a past verb, go with the past perfect.
